Let’s talk about something that might feel all too familiar— that critical inner voice we sometimes call the “madwoman in the attic.”
You know, that part of you that keeps whispering, “You’re not enough. You’re not doing enough. You don’t deserve to rest or take care of yourself.”
It’s almost like carrying around a little echo of every expectation you’ve ever faced, every insecurity you’ve ever felt, and every harsh word you’ve ever heard.
For many of us—especially if you’ve grown up believing you have to put everyone else first or always be perfect—this inner critic can be downright relentless.
Maybe you’ve heard it say things like, “You should be able to handle this,” or, “Other people have it way worse, so what right do you have to complain?”
But what if you could turn down the volume on that voice?
Here are a few steps that can really help:
First, try naming the voice. Notice when that self-criticism pops up, and remind yourself—it’s not the real you talking.
Next, respond with compassion. If a friend came to you with those same worries, how would you answer? Try offering yourself that same gentle kindness.
Then, challenge those impossible standards. Ask yourself, “Are these expectations even fair? Or possible?”
And finally, practice self-acceptance. Remember, being human means being imperfect—every single one of us.
Here’s a practical exercise you can try:
Write down the words your critic uses. Then, take a moment to rewrite them as if you were comforting someone you care about deeply.
Over time, this simple practice can soften that harsh inner dialogue, making more room for self-compassion—and real growth.
